issues.issue: The clause makes this policy excess over "any other valid and collectible insurance available to the insured, whether or not described in the Schedule of Underlying Insurance," then imposes a contribution formula for other excess indemnity policies. "Valid and collectible" and the parenthetical carve-out are the terms two insurers would read differently.

The Overlap Endorsement (c115) presupposes disputes between insurers over which policy applies and shifts the insured's expenses to this insurer, which sits awkwardly with this clause's blanket excess-and-contribution scheme. The two provisions allocate the consequences of overlapping cover differently.

The Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c075) adds that the company recovers "only after the insured has been fully compensated for damages," which qualifies this unconditional subrogation right. The two must be read together to know when subrogation attaches.

This apportionment reimburses the excess-paying interest first and only then the insured or underlying insurers, whereas the Wisconsin made-whole amendment (c075) entitles the company to recovery only after the insured is fully compensated. The order of payment stated in the two provisions conflicts.

This condition says notice to or knowledge of an agent works no waiver or change and that terms can be changed only by endorsement, while the Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c076–c077) makes an agent's knowledge the company's knowledge and prevents a known breach from voiding the policy. The two state opposite rules about agent knowledge.

The Cancellation – Wisconsin endorsement (c066) restates cancellation by the named insured in different terms, so two cancellation-by-insured provisions sit in the same policy. Which controls is unstated.

This condition requires thirty days' written notice of company cancellation, while the Cancellation – Wisconsin endorsement (c067–c069) permits ten days and General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100) requires sixty days. Three different notice periods govern the same act.

The delivery-and-refund sentence is broken into fragments ("shall be sufficient ... any refund due the named insured") and neither the proof-of-mailing rule nor the refund calculation can be read from it. As printed it states no ascertainable rule about premium refund.

The insured warrants that underlying policies or "renewals or replacements thereof not more restricted" will be maintained, and "not more restricted" has no benchmark for comparison. Whether a replacement policy breaches the warranty turns on that phrase.

The deeming rule here (the umbrella applies as if underlying insurance had been maintained) cannot easily be squared with Condition 5 (c045), which withholds attachment until the underlying limit is actually paid. The consequence of a gap in the underlying layer is stated twice, differently.

"Except insofar as coverage is available to the insured in the underlying insurance listed" is a following-form qualifier whose reach depends on what "available" means once the underlying limits are exhausted or the underlying insurer denies. "Liability assumed ... under any contract or agreement" is itself a contested phrase.

The endorsement preserves cover "insofar as coverage is afforded under the underlying insurance or self insured retention listed in Item 7 of the Declarations," but Item 7 is the schedule of underlying insurance and the self-insured retention appears in Item 4. The mis-cited item makes the carve-back's operation uncertain.

This endorsement removes mental injury, mental anguish, shock, false arrest, malicious prosecution, libel and privacy invasion from "personal injury," which the policy's own definition (c026) expressly includes. The definition and the endorsement point in opposite directions.

The exclusion bars claims "initiated, alleged or caused to be brought about by a Named Insured ... against any other Named Insured," and "caused to be brought about" has no clear boundary. Whether a claim assigned or encouraged by one insured is caught is left open.

The policy creates several tiers of insured — Named Insureds (c093), additional insureds (c096) and persons who are insureds only under underlying policies (c023) — and this endorsement speaks only of "Named Insured," so its reach across those tiers is unresolved. The definitional structure and the exclusion do not line up.

This proviso operates only "if this policy applies to professional liability," yet the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089) excludes professional health care services altogether subject to its own exception (c090). Whether the condition is ever satisfied cannot be answered from this clause alone.

Condition 12 (c055) also provides for cancellation by the named insured in different words, leaving two overlapping provisions on the same subject. Which text governs surrender versus mailed notice is unstated.

The ten-day notice permitted here conflicts with the thirty days in Condition 12 (c056) and the sixty days promised by General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100). The policy states three different periods for company cancellation.

General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100) promises sixty days' written notice "in the event of cancellation or non-renewal" without excepting non-payment, which contradicts the ten-day period allowed here. The two notice rules cannot both apply to a premium default.

Cancellation is permitted for "substantial change in the risk assumed" and "substantial breaches of contractual duties, conditions or warranties," neither of which is given any measure of substantiality. The grounds are stated at a level of generality that would have to be construed.

The ten-day period stated here conflicts with the sixty-day notice guaranteed by General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100) and with the thirty days in Condition 12 (c056). The three provisions give different answers for the same mid-term cancellation.

This paragraph addresses policies "written without a fixed expiration date or for a policy term longer than one year," but the declarations (c004) fix a one-year term, so it has no application to this policy. The mismatch is apparent but consequence-free.

The insured is given "a right to renewal of this policy on the terms then being applied by the Company to similar risks," and neither "similar risks" nor the terms so applied are ascertainable from the instrument. The content of the renewal right is left open.

This makes "full compliance by the insured with all the terms of this policy" a condition precedent to suit, while the Declarations paragraph of the same endorsement (c079) says no failure of a pre-loss condition affects the company's obligation unless it increases the risk or contributes to the loss. The two paragraphs of one endorsement state opposite consequences for breach.

"Any person or organization or the legal representative thereof shall be entitled to recover under this policy" is unqualified and appears to give strangers to the contract a direct right of recovery. The absence of any limiting words is the defect.

This entitlement sits against the no-joinder sentence (c048), which bars any person from joining the company in an action, and against the full-compliance condition precedent (c072) in the same endorsement. Whether third parties may sue directly cannot be answered without reconciling all three.

The made-whole rule contradicts the apportionment order in Condition 10 (c053), which reimburses the excess-paying interest first and the insured only out of any remaining balance. The two cannot both control the distribution of a recovery.

Imputing an agent's knowledge to the company is the opposite of Condition 11 (c054), which provides that notice to or knowledge of any agent works no waiver or change. The two provisions state incompatible rules.

The provision repeats the preceding agent-knowledge sentence before adding the non-avoidance rule, so the same words appear twice within one clause. The duplication obscures which sentence carries the operative rule.

The rule that a breach known to the agent "shall not void the policy or defeat a recovery" cannot be squared with the condition-precedent requirement of full compliance in c072. One forgives known breaches, the other bars suit for any breach.

This provision forgives failures of pre-loss conditions unless they increase the risk or contribute to the loss, directly cutting across the "full compliance ... condition precedent" requirement in c072 and the notice condition in c041. The policy states two inconsistent consequences for breach of condition.

The exclusion reaches acts or omissions "of any insured subject of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act ... with respect to their duties under pension or Employee benefit plans," and the mangled "insured subject of" leaves the class of excluded actors unclear. Whether it is fiduciary status or plan-related duty that triggers the exclusion is not stated cleanly.

Limb (b) excludes damage to "property used by any Insured hereunder" without any qualification, an extraordinarily broad category next to the narrower owned/occupied and care-custody-control limbs. The general limb's reach against the specific ones is genuinely contestable.

The base policy exclusion (c022) limits the care, custody or control exclusion to property "to the extent the insured is under contract to provide insurance," a qualifier this endorsement drops. The two versions of the property exclusion differ in scope.

The endorsement says "directors and officers are excluded from this contract for liability arising out of wrongful acts," which reads as excluding persons rather than a class of loss. Whether it removes D&Os as insureds or only removes a category of liability is left ambiguous.

The exception in c085 preserves liability for personal injury, bodily injury, property damage, hospital professional liability and advertisers' liability — essentially everything the policy insures — so the exclusion may have nothing left to operate on. The exclusion and its exception have to be reconciled.

"Wrongful Acts" ends with "or any other matter claimed against them solely by reason of their being directors or officers," a catch-all appended to a list of specific errors and breaches of duty. How far that residual clause reaches beyond the enumerated conduct is the classic ejusdem generis question.

The carve-out restores cover for personal injury, bodily injury, property damage and hospital professional liability, which are the only categories of liability the insuring agreement (c009) covers, so read literally it nullifies the D&O exclusion in c083. The exclusion and exception cannot both be given full effect.

The policy's definition of personal injury (c026(5)) expressly includes "racial or religious discrimination not committed by or on behalf of the insured," which this endorsement wholly removes. The definition and the endorsement point in opposite directions on discrimination claims.

The exclusion's opening words are cut off and the sentence reaches injury "at any time of the manufacture of, or mining of, or use of, or exposure to Asbestos products," leaving the excluded conduct only partially legible. What the exclusion applies to cannot be stated confidently from the text.

The insuring agreement (c010) obliges the company to defend suits not covered by underlying insurance "even if such suit is groundless, false or fraudulent," while this endorsement negates any defence duty for asbestos allegations. The two set different rules for a suit alleging asbestos injury.

The exclusion turns on injury "arising out of the rendering of or failure to render" professional health care services, and the line between professional services and administrative or corporate negligence by a hospital is a standing point of dispute. Limb (b)'s "similar professional board or committee" is a further catch-all of uncertain reach.

Other provisions assume this policy does cover professional liability — the Cross Suits professional-liability proviso (c064), the Aggregate Limits Endorsement's "any professional liability hazard" (c092), the D&O exception's "hospital professional liability" (c085) and the professional liability limits endorsement (c134). A blanket professional services exclusion cannot easily be reconciled with them.

The exception is framed as a double negative — the exclusion "does not apply to those entities or individuals that are not subject to the Wisconsin Patients Compensation Fund" — and "subject to" could mean statutorily required to participate, actually enrolled, or in fact covered for the claim. The class of insureds who keep professional cover turns entirely on that phrase.

The Contingent Excess Medical Malpractice endorsement (c109–c111) draws the same line by reference to Wis. Stat. § 655.001 and its own contingency conditions, and c113 disapplies a differently dated version of this form. Which instrument governs Fund-related entities is not resolved.

This endorsement amends paragraph III to a figure "stated in Item 3 of the declarations," while General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c122) purports to amend "the policy limits in Item 2" to $20,000,000. The two amendments to the limit provision do not reference the same declarations item or the same figure.

The aggregate is extended to loss arising out of "any professional liability hazard," a term that — unlike "products hazard" and "completed operations hazard" — is nowhere defined in the policy. Its reach against those two defined companions is exactly the general-versus-specific problem.

Applying an aggregate to professional liability presupposes that professional liability is covered, which the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089) denies except for entities outside the Wisconsin Fund. The two endorsements cannot both be given their natural reading.

The definition of named insured (c020) automatically includes any subsidiary and any organisation under the named insured's control, whereas this endorsement lists entities individually and denies automatic coverage for newly acquired entities. The two provisions state different rules for affiliate coverage.

Cover for the listed additional insureds runs "only with respect to their interest in the operations of the Named Insured," and several entries describe the insurable interest merely as "As their interest may appear." The extent of each entity's cover is left to be inferred rather than stated.

Seeger Health Resources, Inc. appears both as a Named Insured under c093 and as a mere additional insured here with cover limited to its interest as lessor, so its status under the policy is stated twice and differently. Which characterisation governs is unresolved.

This endorsement restricts the Collection Agency Errors and Omissions Exclusion to Med-Health Financial Services, whereas the form itself (c108) excludes such acts "by or on behalf of the Insured" generally. The scope of that exclusion is stated inconsistently by the two documents.

The sixty-day notice promised here conflicts with the thirty days in Condition 12 (c056) and with the ten-day periods in the Cancellation – Wisconsin endorsement (c067, c068, c069). The policy gives three inconsistent cancellation notice periods.
